title: Inflection and person endings
deck: Latin shows who is doing what by changing the ends of its words. On a verb, the ending tells you who is doing it.
desc: GCSE Latin grammar, Chapter 1: what inflection is, and the six person endings of a Latin verb, with verbs to translate and write.
key: changing a word's ending to change its job
the part of the verb that gives its meaning
the part that says who is doing it

marks.c: the stem: what the verb means
marks.v: the ending: who is doing it

blocks.lead: English mostly uses word order to show who is doing what: "the dog bites the man" means something different from "the man bites the dog". Latin uses the ends of its words instead. Changing the ending of a word to change its job is called inflection.

blocks.p: English still does this a little. "I" becomes "me", "he" becomes "him", and "walk" becomes "walks" after "he". Latin does it with almost every word, so the ending is the first thing to look at.

example.en: He walks, or she walks, or it walks.
example.note: ambula- means "walk". The ending -t says who: he, she or it. One Latin word, two English words.

facts: A Latin verb has a stem, which carries the meaning, and an ending, which tells you who is doing it.
Latin does not need a separate word for "I", "you", "he" or "they": the ending already says it.
So one Latin verb is often two words in English: clamo, "I shout".

blocks.p: There are six endings, one for each person. Every tense you meet later uses the same set, so they are worth knowing by heart.

blocks.note: Say them as one word until they stick: o, s, t, mus, tis, nt. In the first person, the -o takes the place of the stem's last letter: clama- + o is clamo.

sections.h2: Translating a verb on its own

facts: Find the ending first and turn it into the English person: -nt, "they".
Then add the meaning from the stem: navigant, "they sail".
-t can be "he", "she" or "it". On its own any of them is right; in a story, the sentence tells you which.
English has one "you" where Latin has two: -s for one person, -tis for more than one. Both are "you" in English.
-t is one person and -nt is more than one. "They" for clamat loses the mark.
-s and -tis are both "you". Do not mix -tis up with -mus, "we".
There is no separate Latin word for "I" or "he" here: the ending already contains it.

blocks.p: Two short exercises. Type your answer and it is marked against a mark scheme, so you can see which part you have and which you have not. Nothing is saved.

exercise.title: Translate it
exercise.intro: Translate each verb into English. Any natural wording is fine.

trap.say: -tis is "you", more than one of you.

exercise.title: Write the Latin
exercise.intro: Add the right ending to the stem in brackets.

alts.clamant: That is "they shout". One person needs -t: clamat.

alts.pugnatis: That is "you fight", more than one of you. "We" is -mus: pugnamus.

alts.amatis: That is "you" for more than one person. One person takes -s: amas.

items.why: "I" is -o, and it takes the place of the stem's a: saluto.

alts.salutao: The -o takes the place of the a: saluto, not salutao.
